Senses.Explanation: “The command does not run in vain” (令不虛行) says that an issued order or authoritative action takes effect. Zhugan answers with it when asked why his staff leaps to the thirty-third heaven. An Xingfu attaches it to the white staff that strikes morning and evening. Yikui says recognition of his own position makes his command effective; Baichi places “the house expert’s true command” in a verse; Guantaoqi says it after striking the staff; Yi’an repeats it after directing the assembly to look at the place marked by his staff. The grammatical subjects vary between a command, a true command, and Yikui’s command, but each asserts effective execution.

Senses.Explanation: Yanguan Qi’an’s sentence that the ancient buddha passed away long ago first answers a repeated question after a water bottle is moved out and back. Later masters lift the sentence out of that exchange and use it as a fresh answer or hall verdict. Yanguan gives the sentence only after the bottle has been brought and replaced. Zhanran Yuancheng gives it when an official tries to continue after asking for the “golden needle”; Zhenxie Qingliao uses it after warning that a raised eyebrow is already a miss; Cishou Huaishen repeats it as his own closing answer; and Wuming Huijing raises his staff and asks whether the assembly wants another ladle of foul water.

Senses.Explanation: The Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies is the title of a compiled record of earlier masters and their encounters. The title stands on the work’s own volume heading, while later letters, biographies, and textual studies cite it as a book that can be opened, read, purchased, and used as evidence. Mizang Daokai describes an immediate surge on opening it. Hanyue Fazang’s chronology reports that he sought out its volumes and wept over awakening encounters and exchanges between teachers and students. A Complete Five Lamps biography says Yelü Chucai repeatedly brought material learned from it to Sheng’an Cheng. Zen bends no individual word inside this title; its distinctive work is documentary. The collection carries attributed voices into later encounters, where readers cite, test, contest, and reuse them.

Senses.Explanation: An old-temple incense burner is a stock Chan image whose cold, long-unused stillness can be praised, made to blaze or sprout again, or attacked as evidence for a dead-water counterfeit. Jingyin Weiyue pairs one's own field putting out a branch with the old-temple censer's cold ashes blazing again. Later case verses make the same censer produce auspicious grass, so the image is not confined to lifeless stillness. The inherited Shishuang formula also says to go like an old-temple censer. Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes that series beside Yunfeng's opposite command to go amid confused activity. Zhongfeng Mingben supplies the necessary warning: he rebukes students who suppress themselves into deep dead water and then cite 'old-temple censer,' resting, and stopping as proof.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古曲無音韻，如何和得齊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin (天隱和尚語錄): Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the question how an ancient tune without pitch can be harmonized.

Senses.Explanation: The ancient tune is an inherited song-image that masters test through silence, present-day resonance, responsive singing, and the claim that it is not musical pitch at all. Ruti answers a question about the old tuning by remaining silent, then verses that the ancient tune sounds powerfully and its present rhythm is the same. Zhongfeng Mingben places its mysterious sound on the Taiyang road; the Patriarchs' Hall raises Ruti's verse and asks what the line about buddhas losing the trail accomplishes. Later records ask how a tune without pitch can be harmonized and criticize inherited answers. Another verse states directly that the ancient tune is not musical pitch. The title 'Fengxue's Ancient Tune' indexes this same case family rather than a second lexical meaning.

Senses.Explanation: The scale weight is the dense iron counterweight used in weighing. Masters exploit that physical hardness and fixed weight in public answers: Mingjue Cong calls it seven catties; Guyin Yuncong and Quanan Qiji say that stepping on it is hard as iron. Tian’an Sheng and Qigang Zong deliberately force the impossible image further, pressing the iron weight for golden juice or oil. The corpus keeps the concrete implement visible while using its resistant material in replies and attached verses.
